latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Insufficient alveolar macrophage, neutrophil, and T-cell control of inhaled Aspergillus conidia. This activity is raised by prolonged neutropenia, hematologic malignancy, transplant immunosuppression, corticosteroids, chronic lung disease, severe viral lung injury, diabetes, and critical illness.

Transition from inhaled or sinus-trapped conidia to germinating hyphae on injured airway epithelium, alveoli, or sinonasal mucosa. This is the gateway from colonization or fungal ball to invasive disease.

Septate hyphae invade bronchial mucosa, alveoli, lung parenchyma, sinus tissue, orbit, bone, or other sterile tissues. This mechanism drives tissue diagnosis, galactomannan release, beta-D-glucan elevation, local necrosis, and progression despite antibacterial therapy.

Aspergillus hyphae invade vessel walls, causing thrombosis, hemorrhagic infarction, cavitation, hemoptysis, pulmonary arterial thrombi, stroke, and tissue necrosis. This is a central mortality mechanism in invasive aspergillosis.
Lung-dominant invasive disease with nodules, halo sign, ground-glass opacity, consolidation, cavitation, airway-invasive bronchiolitis, hypoxemia, and respiratory failure.

Invasive Aspergillus spreads from paranasal sinuses into orbital apex, cavernous sinus, skull base, optic canal, bone, and adjacent cranial structures. Clinical output includes headache, orbital pain, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, optic neuropathy, and cranial vascular invasion.
Vascular invasion seeds brain, skin, kidney, heart, liver, spleen, or other sterile sites. CNS disease may appear as abscesses, infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, meningitis, or altered mental status.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic inflammatory and organ dysfunction response
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Host inflammatory response and organ dysfunction caused by invasive fungal tissue infection, pulmonary failure, angioinfarction, coinfection, and delayed active antifungal therapy. Fever and CRP may be blunted in neutropenia or high-dose steroid exposure.
Azole resistance, delayed active antifungal therapy, poor absorption, drug interactions, inadequate tissue penetration, or absent source control sustaining hyphal burden despite treatment.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Alveolar macrophages and neutrophils normally kill inhaled conidia; impaired defense permits germination.
Germinating Aspergillus hyphae invade damaged epithelium and sterile tissue when host containment fails.
Aspergillus is angioinvasive; vessel wall penetration creates thrombosis, hemorrhage, infarction, and necrosis.
Most invasive aspergillosis starts in lung or airway tissue and becomes visible as nodules, consolidation, or cavitation.
Sinonasal invasive disease can extend through bone and vessel walls into orbit, optic canal, cavernous sinus, and skull base.
Vascular invasion allows hematogenous spread to brain and other organs.
Tissue-invasive fungal infection generates fever, acute-phase response, and organ dysfunction, although response may be blunted by steroids or neutropenia.
Absent active therapy, azole resistance, underdosing, or low exposure sustains hyphal growth and tissue invasion.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Fever may be absent with corticosteroids, neutropenia, advanced age, or critical illness.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Fever is common but nonspecific in invasive aspergillosis.
Fever, hypoxemia, and systemic stress raise heart rate.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: CRP may be less discriminating when bacterial coinfection, interstitial lung disease flare, or steroid blunting coexists.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Invasive tissue infection produces an acute-phase response.
Pure invasive aspergillosis usually has lower procalcitonin than bacterial sepsis, but coinfection and shock can raise it.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Non-neutropenic steroid, transplant, COPD, ICU, or diabetes-associated cases may have normal or high neutrophil count.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Prolonged neutropenia is a major host state for invasive aspergillosis but not required.
Airway and parenchymal invasion commonly causes cough, sometimes with sputum.
Parenchymal disease, hypoxemia, and respiratory failure manifest as dyspnea.
Hypoxemia and pulmonary inflammation raise respiratory drive.
Nodular, airway-invasive, or diffuse parenchymal disease impairs gas exchange.
Severe pulmonary IPA can progress to acute hypoxemic respiratory failure or ARDS.
CT may show nodules, consolidation, ground glass, tree-in-bud, or diffuse infiltrates.
Well-circumscribed nodules are a classic CT feature of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
Ground-glass halo around a nodule reflects perilesional hemorrhage in angioinvasive disease.
Necrosis and immune recovery can cavitate invasive nodules.
Air crescent commonly appears later as necrotic tissue separates during neutrophil recovery.
Vascular invasion and cavitation can produce hemoptysis, including massive bleeding.
Invasive mold burden can raise serum beta-D-glucan, though the marker is not species-specific.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Sensitivity is highest in neutropenic hematology hosts and lower in non-neutropenic airway-invasive disease.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Growing Aspergillus hyphae release galactomannan into serum.
BAL galactomannan is a strong mycologic axis for pulmonary invasive aspergillosis.
Invasive sino-orbital disease usually originates in paranasal sinus mucosa.
Fungal tissue invasion can form an orbital apex, skull-base, or sinus mass with bone erosion.
Orbital apex involvement causes optic neuropathy and ophthalmoplegia.
Sinus, skull-base, orbital, or CNS invasion often presents with persistent headache or orbital pain.
Optic canal, orbital apex, or cavernous sinus invasion can cause irreversible vision loss.
Cerebral aspergillosis often appears as multiple abscess-like or infarcted lesions.
CNS lesions, hypoxemia, sepsis physiology, or adrenal/metabolic context can cause altered mental status.
Diffuse pulmonary IPA can produce severe hypoxemic respiratory failure.
Vascular dissemination to CNS markedly worsens prognosis.
Cavitary angioinvasive lesions can erode vessels and cause life-threatening hemorrhage.
Cavernous sinus or carotid invasion and hematogenous vascular invasion can occlude cerebral arteries.
Mortality rises with respiratory failure, shock physiology, delayed therapy, and host frailty.
Angioinvasion causes infarction, pulmonary hemorrhage, stroke, and disseminated disease.
CNS or multiorgan dissemination is a high-mortality invasive aspergillosis state.
Added during horizontal ontology audit: this axis is a real shared inflammatory/CNS involvement feature for this disease family, not a case-specific ranking patch.

Tachycardia reflects fever, hypoxemia, systemic inflammation, shock, or respiratory distress.
Historical fever may be more informative than current measured temperature when antipyretics, steroids, or ED timing blunt the snapshot.
Rigors or chills can occur with invasive fungal infection but are less specific than lung/sinus imaging and mycologic context.
Rises with pulmonary involvement, hypoxemia, and systemic stress.

Pulmonary disease, hypoxemia, airway obstruction, or underlying lung disease can produce dyspnea.

Nonspecific systemic symptom from inflammatory burden, hypoxemia, malignancy, or chronic immunosuppression.

May reflect CNS aspergillosis, hypoxemia, shock, metabolic disturbance, or drug toxicity.
Can be low with marrow suppression/neutropenia, normal in transplant hosts, or high with steroid effect and bacterial coinfection.
Profound neutropenia strongly raises prior and changes CT phenotype; non-neutropenic disease remains possible.
Lymphopenia marks impaired cellular immunity and steroid effect.

Thrombocytopenia from hematologic disease, sepsis physiology, medications, or DIC increases bleeding/procedure risk.
Often elevated but nonspecific; may be high from bacterial coinfection or underlying inflammatory lung disease.
Usually lower than bacterial sepsis in isolated Aspergillus disease; high values suggest bacterial coinfection, shock, or severe critical illness.
Fungal cell-wall marker; supportive but nonspecific and may be elevated by other invasive fungi or false-positive contexts.
Serum galactomannan optical density index; sensitivity highest in neutropenic hematology hosts and lower in non-neutropenic airway disease.
BAL galactomannan optical density index; a high respiratory-compartment marker when bronchoscopy is feasible.
Aspergillus isolated from sputum/BAL; interpretation depends strongly on host state and imaging because colonization is possible.
Respiratory or tissue Aspergillus PCR probability; best used with host and imaging context.
Renal impairment modifies amphotericin toxicity, antifungal dosing, and host reserve; may reflect baseline CKD or AKI.
Renal and catabolic reserve marker relevant to amphotericin and critical illness.
Low albumin marks frailty, inflammation, malnutrition, liver disease, or critical illness.
Baseline hepatic injury and azole hepatotoxicity axis.
Hepatic dysfunction modifies azole selection and toxicity.
Diabetes or steroid-induced hyperglycemia raises invasive fungal infection risk and worsens outcomes.
Parent lung imaging burden axis for nodules, consolidation, ground glass, airway-invasive bronchiolitis, or diffuse infiltrates.
Macronodules or multiple nodules on CT are common in invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
Ground-glass halo surrounding a pulmonary nodule; supportive early angioinvasive pattern.
Cavitary transformation of invasive nodules from necrosis or immune recovery.
Late crescent of air around necrotic tissue; often follows neutrophil recovery and is not an early rule-in requirement.
Ground-glass component may be halo, diffuse inflammatory infiltrate, or underlying lung disease overlap.
Usually absent or modest in isolated IPA; large effusion suggests coinfection, malignancy, renal/cardiac overload, or alternate disease.
Paranasal sinus disease is the parent finding for sino-orbital invasive aspergillosis.
Orbital, skull-base, sphenoid fissure, optic canal, or pterygopalatine invasive soft tissue process with or without bone erosion.
Focal osteolysis or skull-base/orbital bony destruction from invasive fungal spread.
Composite orbital apex syndrome: optic neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, pain, and cranial nerve dysfunction.
Optic nerve sheath enhancement, optic canal involvement, optic atrophy, or radiologic optic nerve damage.
Cerebral aspergillosis as abscess-like, cystic, infarcted, or enhancing lesions.
Probability that current antifungal regimen has meaningful activity at the site of disease.
Context axis for isolate/species susceptibility and expected voriconazole activity.
Context axis for expected isavuconazole activity and azole resistance cross-pattern.
Context axis for amphotericin activity; Aspergillus terreus and some resistant isolates lower this probability.

High when ANC is under about 0.5 x10^9/L or neutropenia is expected to be prolonged.
Corticosteroid, calcineurin inhibitor, antimetabolite, chemotherapy, biologic, or transplant immunosuppression burden.
COPD, bronchiectasis, fibrotic interstitial pneumonia, post-tuberculosis cavities, or other damaged-airway context that raises airway-invasive phenotype.

Completeness of debridement/drainage/resection relative to active invasive focus.
Context for amphotericin toxicity, flucytosine/azole dosing, and critical illness reserve.
Context for azole exposure, hepatotoxicity, and drug-interaction risk.
Context for azole selection and monitoring.
Risk of ARDS or severe hypoxemic respiratory failure from diffuse pulmonary IPA or coinfection.
Risk of requiring invasive ventilation from pulmonary IPA, ARDS, shock, or neurologic decline.
Risk of major hemoptysis or pulmonary hemorrhage from angioinvasion and cavitary lesions.
Risk of CNS abscess, infarct, meningitis, or mycotic aneurysm from hematogenous or skull-base extension.
Risk of large-vessel or small-vessel ischemic stroke due to vascular invasion, cavernous sinus/carotid involvement, or CNS dissemination.
Risk of permanent vision loss from orbital apex, optic nerve, cavernous sinus, or ocular involvement.
AKI risk from critical illness, shock, amphotericin exposure, calcineurin inhibitors, or baseline CKD.
Bleeding risk from biopsy, sinus/orbital debridement, lung resection, or CNS drainage, modified by thrombocytopenia and anticoagulation.

Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from pulmonary failure, angioinvasion, CNS dissemination, delayed active antifungal therapy, host immune deficit, renal/hepatic reserve, and source-control feasibility.
Nonspecific systemic inflammatory marker that commonly rises in clinically significant pulmonary, metastatic, or disseminated infection; included through horizontal fairness audit.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Hypoxemia and tachypnea co-vary in pulmonary IPA.
Worsening gas exchange raises ARDS risk.
Falling SpO2 increases ventilatory support risk.
Mechanical ventilation need marks severe pulmonary failure and high mortality.
Cavitary lesions can erode adjacent vessels.
Hemoptysis is a warning sign for major pulmonary hemorrhage.
Major pulmonary hemorrhage is an immediate high-mortality complication.
Brain abscess confirms CNS event space and drives recurrent/progressive CNS hazard.
CNS aspergillosis has very high mortality.
Orbital apex involvement threatens optic nerve function.
Skull-base and cavernous sinus extension can involve the carotid artery or intracranial vessels.
Early active antifungal exposure reduces hyphal burden and downstream fatal events.
Adequate debridement or drainage reduces persistent invasive focus when source control is relevant.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Adequate isolate susceptibility and exposure are required for reliable hyphal killing.
Azole resistance or suspected environmental resistance can make voriconazole inactive.
Hepatic impairment raises exposure and hepatotoxicity risk.

failure_modes: delayed initiation after tissue invasion is advanced
subtherapeutic trough from poor absorption or drug interactions
hepatotoxicity or neurovisual toxicity limiting exposure
treatments.context_specific_role: Systemic anti-hyphal therapy with CNS and pulmonary penetration when exposure is adequate; requires therapeutic drug monitoring where available.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Expected isolate susceptibility and adequate exposure are required for effect.
Isavuconazole usually shortens rather than prolongs QTc.

failure_modes: delayed use in rapidly progressive disease
treatments.context_specific_role: Systemic anti-Aspergillus triazole option when toxicity, QT, renal formulation context, or drug interactions make it suitable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Species and isolate context determine amphotericin activity.
Renal impairment increases nephrotoxicity cost and may constrain dosing.

side_effects.interpretation: renal toxicity enters outcome through AKI hazard

treatments.context_specific_role: Systemic polyene path when azole resistance, severe intolerance, pregnancy context, or rapidly progressive disease makes a non-azole active path necessary.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cross-resistance can make salvage azoles ineffective.

treatments.context_specific_role: Continuation or salvage azole path when susceptibility, exposure, and toxicity context support it.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Echinocandins are not sufficient as a lone causal path for most invasive aspergillosis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct or salvage anti-hyphal pressure in selected severe, resistant, or intolerance contexts.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Surgery has causal benefit when a focal necrotic sinus/orbital/brain/lung source is present.
Thrombocytopenia, anticoagulation, or vascular invasion can make procedures dangerous.

failure_modes: incomplete debridement due to skull-base/orbital anatomy
continued immunosuppression and residual necrotic tissue
treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical reduction of necrotic fungal burden when anatomy and host reserve make source control feasible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Reducing steroids or antimetabolites can restore macrophage/neutrophil function but may risk graft rejection or disease flare.

failure_modes: graft rejection or immune disease flare
immune reconstitution inflammatory worsening around lesions

side_effects.interpretation: immune reconstitution can transiently worsen inflammatory lung injury

treatments.context_specific_role: Host-defense restoration path when immunosuppression can be safely reduced.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Neutrophil recovery is most relevant when profound neutropenia is present.

failure_modes: worsening inflammatory lung lesions during recovery

side_effects.interpretation: radiographic immune-recovery cavitation can appear as lesions evolve

treatments.context_specific_role: Host neutrophil restoration path in prolonged neutropenia, coordinated with hematology constraints.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Supportive oxygenation is used when gas exchange is impaired.

side_effects.interpretation: ventilator-associated infection risk when invasive ventilation is required

treatments.context_specific_role: Bridge for hypoxemic respiratory failure while antifungal and source-control paths act.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluid supports perfusion when shock physiology or hypovolemia is present.

failure_modes: pulmonary edema in severe lung disease
treatments.context_specific_role: Hemodynamic bridge for shock overlap; does not treat fungal burden.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vasopressor supports perfusion during septic or vasodilatory shock.

failure_modes: digital or mesenteric ischemia at high dose

side_effects.interpretation: high catecholamine state may worsen ischemic vulnerability but is usually necessary in shock

treatments.context_specific_role: Perfusion bridge for shock physiology while causal therapy acts.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: KRT supports severe AKI complications and changes antifungal exposure but does not kill Aspergillus.

side_effects.interpretation: dialysis catheter and anticoagulation bleeding risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Renal support for severe AKI, uremia, refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, or volume overload.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises invasive pulmonary and sino-orbital disease probability; inflammatory response may be muted and azole-calcineurin inhibitor interactions become important.

copd_bronchiectasis_or_interstitial_lung.trajectory_modulation: Raises airway-invasive and atypical consolidation phenotype; classic halo sign may be absent.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises ICU-associated pulmonary aspergillosis risk with nonspecific infiltrates and frequent bacterial/viral coinfection.

uncontrolled_or_new_steroid_induced.trajectory_modulation: Impaired neutrophil function and tissue repair raise invasive sinonasal, pulmonary, and disseminated risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises sino-orbital invasive pathway, especially after antibiotics, corticosteroids, surgery, diabetes, or immunosuppression.

early_active_therapy.trajectory_modulation: Lower hyphal plateau and complication hazards.

delay_after_progressive_radiology_or_pos.trajectory_modulation: Higher angioinvasion, dissemination, respiratory failure, and mortality hazard.

supportive_care: Obtain high-resolution chest CT early when invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is suspected; repeat imaging if symptoms or oxygenation worsen despite antibacterial therapy.

Send serum galactomannan, serum beta-D-glucan, respiratory culture, BAL galactomannan/PCR when feasible, and tissue biopsy when safely possible; interpret respiratory Aspergillus isolation with host and imaging context.

Do not treat respiratory Aspergillus culture as colonization by default in high-risk hosts with compatible imaging; also do not use culture alone as ordinary presentation evidence when tissue invasion is the confirmatory fact.

Assess host state explicitly: ANC trajectory, corticosteroid dose, transplant medications, chemotherapy, hematologic malignancy, chronic lung disease, diabetes, ICU viral pneumonia, and prior azole exposure.

Start active systemic antifungal therapy promptly when clinical, imaging, and host evidence strongly support invasive aspergillosis; refine using species, susceptibility, and therapeutic drug monitoring.
Therapeutic drug monitoring for voriconazole and posaconazole when available; monitor hepatic enzymes, QTc, neurovisual effects, and calcineurin inhibitor interactions.
Monitor amphotericin nephrotoxicity with creatinine, potassium, magnesium, volume status, and concurrent nephrotoxins.
Evaluate for dissemination when neurologic symptoms, sinus/orbital signs, skin lesions, persistent fever, or angioinvasive imaging is present; use brain MRI when CNS disease is suspected.
For sino-orbital or skull-base disease, coordinate infectious diseases, ENT, ophthalmology, neurosurgery, radiology, and transplant/hematology teams for debridement feasibility and vision/CNS risk.
Reduce corticosteroids or other immunosuppression when clinically feasible; coordinate with transplant or autoimmune-disease teams to balance rejection or flare risk.
Support oxygenation with low-flow oxygen, high-flow oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, invasive ventilation, or extracorporeal support according to gas exchange and goals of care.
Use hemodynamic and renal organ-support bundles when shock or AKI develops, but keep antifungal activity and source control as the causal treatment path.
